description: We are a group of passionate Aerospace Engineering undergraduate students at the Sapienza University of Rome. After our bachelor's degree, we intend to pursue a master's degree in Space and Astronautical Engineering, and then build a career in the space industry.
summary: Perseus is an innovative intelligence framework that identifies ideal landing sites on the Moon and Mars, alongside their current and future terrestrial analogues. Developed to bridge deep-space mission planning with real-world field-testing, Perseus relies on two core engines: Sybil, a MATLAB-based unsupervised Machine Learning tool that ranks landing sites and analogs based on rigorous engineering constraints such as slope, rock abundance, and thermal inertia, and Iris, a Python-based spatial processing tool utilizing Google Earth Engine to pinpoint and map potential testing regions interactively. Built using MATLAB, Python, and Google Earth Engine, all components are integrated into a custom interactive web platform featuring dynamic maps and algorithm interfaces. By automating site selection and risk assessment, Perseus accelerates mission design for programs like Artemis and Mars exploration, serving as a scalable decision-support tool that unifies heavy mathematical machine learning and satellite remote sensing into a seamless geospatial web experience.
details: Perseus is an innovative, dual-engine intelligence framework designed to identify, rank, and validate ideal landing sites on the Moon and Mars, as well as their high-fidelity terrestrial analogues—including potential future testing analogues on Earth that are currently undocumented in scientific literature. The project operates through two core, interconnected computational tools: Sybil, an unsupervised Machine Learning and numerical algorithm tool developed in MATLAB, which processes and analyzes different mission parameters (such as landing/touchdown, rover mobility, full lunar base, habitat, lava-tube EVAs, and power/ISRU) to rigorously rank candidate landing sites and their corresponding terrestrial testing grounds based on engineering safety, geological diversity, thermophysics, and scientific value; and Iris, a planetary-scale remote sensing discovery pipeline powered by Google Earth Engine (GEE), which enforces a strict 50 km Haversine exclusion buffer around every known Sybil site, screens hundreds of thousands of equal-area global grid cells using multi-sensor orbital telemetry (from 2021 to 2024), and projects newly characterized abiotic and cryogenic terrains into Sybil's calibrated latent space to uncover previously uncatalogued terrestrial analogues. To build and run Perseus, the team utilized a robust mix of languages, software, and remote data infrastructure, including MATLAB for Sybil's unsupervised machine learning and clustering, Python for Iris and Google Earth Engine satellite data processing, open planetary and Earth catalogs integrating mission data from NASA, ESA, ISRO, JAXA, and ECMWF, as well as a fully interactive web platform, a standalone Leaflet satellite viewer with CSV/GeoJSON export capabilities, and Google Earth KML layers. The intended impact of Perseus is to bridge the gap between deep-space mission planning and terrestrial field-testing by automating the site-selection process and evaluating complex mission constraints—such as slope stability, thermal inertia, illumination geometry, boulder distribution, and regolith mechanics—to drastically reduce the time, cost, and risk associated with mission design, serving as an open-source, scalable decision-support system for researchers, engineers, and space agencies preparing for missions like Artemis and Mars exploration. Perseus is creative because it unifies heavy mathematical machine learning and satellite remote sensing into a seamless, bidirectional global discovery system rather than relying on static, poorly characterized site lists, translating complex orbital telemetry into an accessible, interactive geospatial web experience. When developing the project, Team Perseus carefully considered the multi-domain realities of planetary environments by accounting for diverse environmental facets including topography, geology, thermophysics, radiation, and regolith mechanics, balancing "hard" survival constraints (such as slope limits, maximum boulder size, and rock abundance thresholds) with "soft" operational and scientific criteria (such as geological diversity, resource accessibility, and water-ice potential), and accounting for fundamental differences between planetary bodies by applying pooled Z-score normalization for the lunar pipeline while decoupling Mars' extreme barometric baseline from Earth's via separate domain Z-score standardization so atmospheric pressure differentials do not mask surface geology.
